[THOUGHT]  
The clinical picture centers on persistent, painless, erythematous, crusted lesions at two anatomic sites — penile shaft and left middle finger — with biopsy-proven high-grade squamous intraepithelial neoplasia (HSIL-like changes): nuclear hyperchromasia, multinucleation, and increased mitoses in follicle-bearing epithelium. Critically, the histopathology is *not* consistent with syphilis (which would show plasma cell–rich perivascular inflammation, endarteritis, and often spirochetes on special stain — none reported), nor with HSV (which causes cytopathic effect: ballooning degeneration, intranuclear inclusions, necrosis — not described), nor with fungal or mycobacterial infection (no mention of hyphae, granulomas, AFB, or suppuration). The bilateral involvement (genital + digital) strongly suggests a transmissible, epitheliotropic viral process — most plausibly high-risk HPV infection driving dysplasia at both sites. While digital lesions are less common than genital ones in HPV-related neoplasia, periungual and digit-confined PeIN-like lesions are documented, especially in immunocompetent individuals with high-risk HPV (e.g., HPV16). The negative RPR/TPPA and HIV tests robustly exclude active syphilis and HIV as drivers — eliminating two major mimics of chronic genital ulceration/dysplasia. The absence of systemic symptoms, normal immune status (inferred from negative HIV and lack of opportunistic infections), and lack of nutritional deficiency symptoms make acrodermatitis enteropathica or severe vitamin deficiency unlikely — especially since the histology shows *neoplastic* (not just psoriasiform or acanthotic) change. Pending ancillary studies (HPV PCR, p16) are highly likely to confirm HPV association; p16 overexpression would strongly support HPV-driven dysplasia, and Ki-67 would corroborate high proliferative activity. Thus, the simplest, most parsimonious, and histopathologically best-supported diagnosis is HPV-associated high-grade squamous intraepithelial neoplasia — specifically penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN) grade 2–3, with possible synchronous digital intraepithelial neoplasia.
